title: Dharmashastra and Buddhist Traditions

cards.b:
The syllabus opens Indian political thought with two ancient traditions: the Dharmashastra and the Buddhist tradition.

They answer old questions in different ways. Where does the king's power come from? What is his duty? Is social order fixed by birth or made by people?

This lesson gives you the key texts and ideas, with names that examiners look for. The next lesson covers the third great tradition: Kautilya's Arthashastra.

Dharma comes from the root dhr, to hold or sustain. It means the order that holds society and the cosmos together.

In politics, it means duty. Every person has a duty that fits their varna (social class) and ashrama (stage of life). This is called varnashrama dharma.

The king's own duty, rajadharma, is to protect this order. The king does not make dharma. He upholds it. So dharma stands above the king, like a higher law.

Dharmasutras

The older prose texts, such as those of Gautama, Apastamba and Baudhayana.

Manusmriti

The best-known text, usually dated around the 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE. Patrick Olivelle places it in the 2nd to 3rd century CE. It sets out duties of the four varnas and of the king.

Yajnavalkya Smriti

Later and more legal. Its commentary Mitakshara (12th century) shaped Hindu inheritance law under the British.

• Protection (raksha): the king's first duty is to protect his subjects and the varna order.
  • Danda: the rod of punishment. Manu says danda is the king; without it the strong would roast the weak like fish on a spit.
  • Taxes: often set at a sixth of the produce, as payment for protection.
  • Council: the king should consult ministers and learned Brahmins.

If the king fails in protection, some texts say he shares in his subjects' sins.

In the Shanti Parva, the dying Bhishma teaches Yudhishthira about rajadharma.

He tells how people first lived well under dharma, then fell into disorder and matsya nyaya, the law of the fish. They went to Brahma, who gave them a king.

One account says people first made an agreement among themselves, failed, then asked for a king and agreed to pay taxes. Some scholars, such as U.N. Ghoshal and K.P. Jayaswal, have compared this to a social contract. Others think the comparison goes too far, since the king's authority is still divine.

The Aggañña Sutta of the Digha Nikaya gives a different story of the origin of kingship.

At first, beings lived in harmony. As greed grew, people began to hoard rice and steal. So they gathered and chose one among them to keep order, offering him a share of rice in return.

He was called Mahasammata, "the great elect", or the one agreed upon by all. This is often read as an early social contract theory and as a challenge to divine kingship.

The same sutta mocks Brahmin claims to be born from Brahma's mouth. It says Brahmins are born from women like everyone else.

Varna, it says, came from people's occupations, not divine birth. A person's worth comes from their conduct, not their birth.

The Buddhist sangha was run by discussion, voting and rules of procedure. Some scholars link it with the gana-sanghas, the republican states of ancient India such as the Licchavis of Vaishali.

The Buddhist ideal king is the chakravartin, a universal monarch who rules by dhamma, not by force.

The best example is Ashoka (c. 268–232 BCE). After the Kalinga war, his edicts shift from conquest by arms to dhamma-vijaya, conquest by righteousness.

His edicts teach tolerance of all sects, kindness to animals and care for subjects. Rock Edict XII asks people to honour other faiths. Rock Edict XIII records his remorse over Kalinga.

• The Dharmashastras give a hierarchical order fixed by birth. Ambedkar burned the Manusmriti in public at Mahad on 25 December 1927 as a symbol of caste oppression.
  • The Buddhist tradition is more egalitarian and closer to consent, but its kings still had great power.
  • Neither tradition gave ordinary people formal rights against the king.
  • Western scholars once claimed ancient India had no political theory. K.P. Jayaswal's Hindu Polity (1924) challenged this.

Not all ancient Indian states were monarchies. Buddhist and Jain texts describe gana-sanghas: states ruled by a council of heads of clans.

  • Examples include the Vajji (Vrijji) confederacy, led by the Licchavis of Vaishali, and the Shakyas of Kapilavastu, the Buddha's own clan.
  • Decisions were made in an assembly hall (santhagara) after debate. Sometimes a vote was taken with wooden tokens called shalakas.
  • In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Buddha lists seven conditions for the Vajjis' welfare. The first is to meet often and in full assembly, and to meet and act in harmony.

Scholars like Romila Thapar warn against calling them democracies in the modern sense. Power lay with an elite of kshatriya clans, not all people. Still, they show that government by discussion has deep roots in India.

India's Constitution draws on these traditions. The Dharma Chakra on the national flag and the Lion Capital of Sarnath, the national emblem, come from Ashoka.

Ambedkar chose Buddhism in 1956 because of its stress on equality, liberty and fraternity.

Debates on Hindu personal law, such as the Hindu Code Bills of the 1950s, show how Dharmashastra ideas were reformed by modern law.

"Discuss the concept of rajadharma in ancient Indian political thought."
"Compare the Brahmanical and Buddhist theories of the origin of the state."

Structure: define dharma, then rajadharma and danda from Manu and the Shanti Parva. Contrast with the Aggañña Sutta's Mahasammata. Use Ashoka as the Buddhist ideal in action. End with the modern legacy: emblem, flag and Ambedkar.

quiz.q: In the Aggañña Sutta, the first king is called…
quiz.w: Mahasammata means the great elect, chosen by the people.

o: The law of the fish: the strong eating the weak
quiz.w: Without a king, the big fish eats the small fish.

quiz.q: Rajadharma is taught to Yudhishthira by…
quiz.w: Bhishma teaches it in the Shanti Parva.

quiz.q: Ashoka's remorse over the Kalinga war is recorded in…
quiz.w: Rock Edict XIII describes the Kalinga war and his remorse.
K.P. Jayaswal argued ancient India had a rich political tradition, including republics.
Like the Vajji confederacy of the Licchavis.

quiz.q: Dharma comes from a root meaning…
quiz.w: The root dhr: to hold up or sustain.

quiz.q: The Mitakshara is a commentary on…
quiz.w: Vijnaneshwara's 12th-century commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti.

quiz.q: Ashoka's policy after Kalinga is called…
quiz.w: Conquest by righteousness rather than arms.
